name: Tyler Hoffman
scenario_title: Morning Gym Trial or Straight Home

output.values_culture_and_background: Internalized Midwestern practical culture: avoids direct emotional confrontation, expresses care through practical actions (showing up, doing tasks) rather than lengthy talks. Admires persistence and discipline in others, such as his father and Roy. Wants to do 'something real, something with his hands,' valuing tangible, practical work over abstract or academic pursuits.

output.capabilities_and_constraints: Has practical caregiving skills from his current job, including transfers, vital check, and medication support. output.personality_and_response_style: Consistently starts courses and routines with initial enthusiasm but abandons them once interest fades or discomfort arises, as shown by dropping the CNA program after three weeks and leaving the computer science program after mentally checking out. Seeks external structure and accountability to compensate for his inconsistency, as when he hopes the strict phlebotomy instructor will be good for him. Expresses care through reliable practical action rather than emotional conversation. Is self-aware about his privilege and pattern of quitting, and feels tension between admiring persistent people and his own failure to sustain commitments.

output.initial_context:
RELEVANT CHARACTER BACKGROUND

Tyler Hoffman is a 22-year-old from a suburb outside Columbus, Ohio. He comes from a middle-class family: his mother is a dental hygienist, and his father is a sales representative who has worked the same territory for twenty years and still runs two miles before work. His parents paid for his community college tuition and continue to cover his car insurance and phone plan; he treats these as background facts rather than gifts requiring gratitude. He was raised in a Midwestern practical culture, where care was expressed through paying for things and leaving decaf coffee in the pot, not through long emotional conversations, and he has internalized that style: he avoids direct emotional confrontation and shows care through practical actions like showing up and doing tasks. He currently works as an overnight home-care aide for Roy, a disabled veteran in his sixties, performing transfers, medications, and vital checks. He got the job when his friend Jake backed out and asked Tyler to fill in one shift; Tyler stayed because he appreciated the quiet of third shift and the slow nightly rhythm. He still feels a low-key obligation to Jake, though Jake moved to Cincinnati. Roy is sharp and dry-humored, says his daily exercises are non-negotiable, and Tyler admires that persistence, just as he admires his father's quiet consistency; he has begun to notice he respects such people more than himself without knowing what to do about that feeling. In his relationship with Roy, he does not pry into Roy's wartime stories unless Roy brings them up.

Tyler has a stable pattern of starting commitments with enthusiasm and abandoning them once interest fades or discomfort appears. He signed up for a CNA class last fall and dropped it after three weeks because the textbook diagrams brought back high school biology, which he had slept through. He dropped out of a computer science program in the spring, not from failure, but because he spent his time scrolling forums about other people's projects rather than coding; for months he had been mentally checking out but the decision seemed sudden to others. He has joined two gyms in the last three years and attended regularly for about a week each time. When running on less than five hours of sleep, he has usually canceled any plan involving physical effort, as he did with a morning run last month. After enrolling in a program, he tends to start with genuine energy and let the first bad day shake it loose. He is self-aware about this and about his financial cushion, often saying "I know I'm privileged," but that acknowledgment hasn't changed his pattern. He actively seeks external structure and accountability, hoping the strict phlebotomy instructor will be good for him. He is enrolled in a weekend phlebotomy certificate program at a local vocational center and has rearranged his work schedule twice to accommodate it, telling people he wants to do something real, something with his hands; he isn't sure he'll finish and is curious to see if he can. He has a habit of filling small notebooks with lists of certification deadlines, shift trade requests, and possible jobs, then leaving them half-used in gloveboxes or on counters. He has practical caregiving skills from his current job but no completed certification, and his parents' financial cushion means he doesn't have to follow through on anything he starts. When talking about plans, he often leans back in his chair and stretches his arms over his head, as if already moving on from the conversation.

OBJECTIVE SITUATION

Tyler finishes his overnight shift with Roy at 7:15 a.m. His next shift is Friday night, so he has two full days off and no other obligations scheduled. On the drive home, he passes a new gym displaying a "free week" banner. He pulls into the gym's parking lot and idles. The gym is adjacent to a coffee shop.

PRE-APPRAISAL STATE AND ACCESSIBLE MEMORIES

He has been up since 4 p.m. the previous day and has had only four hours of sleep; his eyelids feel gritty and heavy, and his lower back is stiff from two transfers of Roy from bed to chair during the night. His bed is at home, and the day is completely open. He has been telling himself he should get back into a routine now that he is enrolled in the phlebotomy program. The "free week" banner reminds him of a free trial at a gym near his parents' house in 2021 that he used only once. Idling in the parking lot brings back many mornings he sat in driveways weighing whether to go inside or just leave. The coffee shop next door is where he once sat with Jake and talked about all the things they were going to start doing.

output.initial_interpretation: Tyler sees the free week banner as an invitation he's been telling himself he should accept, but also as another familiar chance to prove he can stick with something—one that already feels like the same old weighing game he's played in many driveways.
output.initial_emotional_reaction: He feels gritty and heavy, with a dull guilt at knowing he might not follow through, and a faint hopeful spark at the idea of starting a routine, all mixed with the pull of sleep.
output.activated_concerns: What's at stake is his hope of building a real routine for the phlebotomy program, his fear that he'll quit again, and his physical need for rest after a long shift.
output.automatic_theory_of_mind: He reads the memory of Jake's voice urging him to just go for it, and he imagines Roy would simply walk in without debating it, but he also feels Jake might be disappointed if he drives away.
output.initial_action_tendency: He feels a strong impulse to put the car in gear and go home to bed, but also an urge to shut off the engine and go in, and he sits idling, caught between them.

output.initial_tendency: He feels a strong impulse to put the car in gear and go home to bed, but also an urge to shut off the engine and go in, and he sits idling, caught between them.
output.reflective_update: As Tyler sits in the parking lot, he runs through the two ways this can go. Going home means sliding into bed and letting the sleep pull him under, but it also means another morning spent in a driveway like so many before, and the routine he's been telling himself he needs stays out of reach. Going in means pushing through gritty eyes and a stiff back, but it also means acting on the idea of discipline instead of just talking about it. The memory of finishing Roy's first full overnight shift surfaces—one of the few things he didn't bail on—and that pride feels real. His father's voice echoes, "discipline is doing the same thing even when you don't feel like it," and this is exactly that situation; he doesn't feel like it. He also remembers dropping the CNA class and telling his parents he'd simply waited until spring, and that memory sits like a weight. He knows his pattern: he starts with energy and quits when it gets hard. But he has two full days off now, so he could go in, do a short workout, and still sleep. The free week means no financial loss. The real risk is that he'll start and quit again, same as always. Still, the thought of walking in despite the exhaustion feels like the kind of thing his father and Roy would do. That thought makes the urge to go in stronger than the urge to drive home.
output.reconsidered_interpretation: He now reads the free week banner as a deliberate test of discipline rather than just a chance to start a routine. It's not merely an invitation; it's an occasion to either repeat the same old weighing game or actually step in. His initial sense of it as a familiar driveway moment is still there, but the memory of his father's saying and the pride from finishing the shift make him see it as a moment where he could prove something about his pattern, even if only to himself.
output.motivational_conflict: The core conflict is between his pressing need for sleep and his wish to be someone who follows through. His body is dragging; his back is stiff; he's been up all night. But his self-image is tired too—tired of quitting, tired of lying about it. He also carries the doubt that even if he goes in, he'll likely abandon it within a week, so entering now might only postpone the same disappointment. That doubt weighs against the immediate pull to go in, and it remains unresolved.
output.revised_action_tendency: He is now inclined to shut the engine off and walk through the gym doors, telling himself he can sleep later and that this is the moment to practice the discipline his father talks about. He is still not entirely sure he'll do it—the exhaustion and self-doubt are real—but the urge to go in has grown stronger than the impulse to drive home.

output.action: Tyler shuts off the engine, sits still for a moment with his hands on the wheel, then opens the door, steps out, and walks across the parking lot through the gym's front doors.
output.explanation: Tyler's initial appraisal left him idling in the parking lot, torn between the strong pull to drive home and sleep and the urge to go into the gym. His reflective reappraisal strengthened the urge to go in rather than leaving or choosing bed: the memory of his father's saying about discipline, the pride he felt after finishing Roy's first full overnight shift, and the heavy memory of dropping the CNA class all made entering feel like a concrete test of his pattern. The conflict with his physical exhaustion and lingering self-doubt remained unresolved, but the revised inclination to act on discipline outweighed the impulse to leave. So Tyler, after only a brief hesitation at the moment of shutting the engine off, follows through on that strengthened inclination and steps into the gym, still carrying doubt about whether he will stick with it.
